paper_reference.citation: Towards Efficient FinBERT via Quantization and Coreset for Financial Sentiment Analysis, FinNLP workshop, EMNLP-2025
paper_reference.note: Coreset selection (their main efficiency contribution) is not replicated here — it matters most at a training-set scale much larger than this dataset's 9,543 rows, where it wasn't the bottleneck. Quantization uses PyTorch's standard dynamic int8 quantization, not the paper's specific multi-bit scheme — a real, reproducible technique, just not a literal replication.

benchmark_ceiling.note: Reports off-the-shelf FinBERT at 0.912 F1 on Financial PhraseBank (a different dataset/label scheme than this script's — not directly comparable, cited for context only) vs. GPU-only instruction-tuned LLMs (FinMA-7B: 0.965, FinGPT: ~0.876) on the same benchmark.

selection_reasoning: The full-precision fine-tuned model is what's shipped (saved to this directory, loaded directly by sentiment_service.py) because it round-trips through standard Hugging Face save/load with zero extra glue code. The quantized variant's accuracy/size tradeoff is measured and reported above for comparison, matching this project's practice of documenting every candidate considered, not just the one shipped (see ml/train_expense_categorizer.py's Logistic Regression vs. Random Forest comparison for the same pattern).
known_limitations: Fine-tuned on short tweets (zeroshot/twitter-financial-news-sentiment), which are stylistically different from full news article text/headlines this model actually scores in production (see sentiment_service.py). Not stress-tested against realistic news-headline text the way Phase 3's expense categorizer was against realistic transaction text — a natural next step if this gap turns out to matter in practice.

Label scheme here (Bearish/Bullish/Neutral) differs from the off-the-shelf FinBERT checkpoint's own (positive/negative/neutral) — this fine-tuned model's outputs use this script's labels, not the base checkpoint's.
